question: A 34-year-old woman rolls her ankle. X-ray shows a fibular fracture 2 cm above the level of the ankle mortise (syndesmosis), with no medial malleolus fracture and no talar shift on mortise view. Which Weber type and management are CORRECT?

answers.text: Weber A — non-operative management with below-knee cast

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Weber A fractures are below the level of the syndesmosis. This fracture is above the syndesmosis — that is Weber C.
Incorrect. Weber B is at the level of the syndesmosis. This fracture is 2 cm above the syndesmosis, making it Weber C. Weber B may be managed non-operatively if the mortise is stable.

answers.text: Weber C — operative fixation because syndesmotic injury is implied

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A fracture above the level of the syndesmosis (Weber C) implies syndesmotic disruption. Even if the mortise appears undisplaced on initial X-ray, Weber C injuries typically require fixation of both the fibula and the syndesmosis.

answers.text: Weber C — non-operative if no talar shift on X-ray

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Absence of talar shift on a non-weight-bearing X-ray does not exclude syndesmotic instability. Weber C injuries require stress X-rays or operative exploration; most require surgical fixation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Weber classification landmarks: the syndesmosis (distal tibiofibular joint) is the reference. A = below, B = at the level, C = above. Weber C implies syndesmotic tear even without obvious talar shift — operative fixation is standard.

Correct. Weber classification: A = below syndesmosis (stable), B = at syndesmosis (variable), C = above syndesmosis (implies syndesmotic disruption, operative). Location of fibular fracture relative to the syndesmosis is the key landmark.
